title: Camera decisions in automatic modes
teaches: Core exposure and focus controls, preset priorities in Bird-watching mode, and manual overrides

blocks.text: **The challenge.** A western bluebird lands on a dead snag at the edge of a clearing, with a leafy bush a few metres behind it. You zoom until the bird fills about a third of the frame, leave the P950 in Bird-watching mode, and press the shutter. The camera gives you the left-hand picture: the bird is sharp, and so is nearly every leaf of the bush behind it, each one competing with the bird for your eye. What you had in mind was the right-hand picture: the same bird, in the same light, on a smooth wash of green and blue with nothing behind it to read.

blocks.caption: The bluebird as Bird-watching mode took it, and as you wanted it

blocks.text: Nothing about the bird, the light or the camera changed between those two pictures, and the camera made no mistake in the first one: it did exactly what its rules say. The difference is a handful of decisions it made without asking, and one it could never make, because you made it with your feet. This lesson follows those decisions and ends with you making the right-hand picture yourself.

Point a camera at a heron and press the shutter button, and the camera makes four physical adjustments in the time it takes you to breathe in. It sets the diameter of the opening in the lens, the time the shutter stays open, the electronic amplification applied to the sensor's signal, and the distance at which the lens brings light to a [[focus|focus]]. Brightness, motion blur, grain, and the span of sharp detail all follow from these four settings.

A scene mode such as Bird-watching applies fixed rules to those adjustments: a short [[shutter|time]] speed (the time the shutter stays open), continuous [[focus|focus]] tracking for a moving animal, and whatever [[ISO|sensor]] setting (the amplification of the sensor's signal) is needed to keep the picture bright enough. Those priorities suit general wildlife work, but the camera applies the same rules in a dim wood at dawn as on a bright shore at noon, without telling you what it gave up.

Each control has an interactive figure below that works on a real photograph: move the slider and the picture changes according to the optics and arithmetic of the [[Nikon Coolpix P950|subject]], the camera used throughout this course.[^p950-specs]

A lens gathers diverging light rays from a scene and bends them back toward a point.[^aperture-etymology] Because a lens can only [[focus|focus]] precisely on a single distance at a time, objects at that exact distance land on the sensor as sharp points, while anything nearer or farther lands as a small blurred disc.[^circle] When that disc is smaller than the sensor can resolve, it still looks like a point and registers as sharp. [[Depth of field|sharp]] is simply the band of distances in the scene whose blur discs remain too small to notice.

blocks.caption: A point source, the cone of light the lens forms from it, and the disc it projects onto the sensor
blocks.task: Move the point off the focused distance, then narrow the aperture until the disc looks sharp again

blocks.text: Narrowing the [[aperture|aperture]] blocks the outer edges of the light cone, which shrinks the blur discs and widens the sharp zone; opening it does the reverse. How smooth a background goes depends on three things: how wide the opening in the lens really is in millimetres (the lens's real focal length divided by the f-number: 357 mm ÷ 6.5, about 55 mm, at the long end, and 4.3 mm ÷ 2.8, about 1.5 mm, at the wide end), how far the background sits behind the subject, and how far you stand from the subject. Zooming in and stepping back to keep the bird the same size in the frame leaves a bush a few metres behind it about as blurred as before, but blurs far hills much more. Because the P950's small sensor uses physically short focal lengths, a soft background takes both the long end of the zoom and a bird with open space behind it.

blocks.caption: The bluebird on its snag, with bushes, pines and hills behind it. Zooming in, you step back so the bird stays the same size.
blocks.task: Make the right-hand picture from the start of the lesson: a smooth background behind a sharp bird

blocks.text: The [[shutter|time]] speed sets how long the sensor collects light.[^muybridge] Anything that moves during that window, whether an animal in the scene or the camera in your hands, records as a streak along its path. Telling those two blurs apart in your own pictures lets you fix the right problem on the next shot: if the whole frame is smeared, the camera moved in your hands; if the bird is smeared against a crisp branch, the bird moved while the camera stayed still.

blocks.caption: A bird in flight, with controls for shutter speed and optical stabilisation
blocks.task: Find a shutter speed that freezes the bird, then turn the stabiliser off to see which blur returns

blocks.text: Optical stabilisation shifts a lens group to counter the tremor of your hands, so it does nothing for a moving bird. Putting the camera on a tripod solves the same hand-shake problem while leaving subject motion untouched. Slow shutter speeds have deliberate uses too: with the camera on a tripod, a long exposure turns rushing water into smooth, misty ribbons.

blocks.caption: A stream photographed from a tripod, so the shutter can stay open as long as the light allows
blocks.task: Use a long shutter speed to draw the water into smooth threads

blocks.text: Light arrives at the camera in discrete packets called photons, and each sensor pixel acts as a bucket that counts how many strike it during the exposure. A pixel that collects ten thousand photons gives a steady measurement of brightness, whereas one that collects only fifty varies wildly from shot to shot because random arrivals fluctuate strongly in a small sample.[^shot-noise] Raising the [[ISO|sensor]] amplifies the voltage read from those pixels after the shutter closes; because it multiplies the small, uneven photon count you already caught, it magnifies the random variations along with the brightness.[^iso-history] That amplified variation shows across the picture as speckled grain or noise.

blocks.caption: The photons a mid-grey tone is counted from at each ISO, and the grain they leave
blocks.task: Raise the ISO until the photon count looks visibly rough

blocks.text: Aperture, shutter speed and ISO all govern the brightness of the photograph, and each carries its own visual trade-off: [[aperture|aperture]] changes depth of field, [[shutter|time]] changes motion blur, and [[ISO|sensor]] changes graininess, because a higher ISO lets the camera get by on less light. Photographers measure exposure in **stops**, where one stop halves or doubles the light. A stop of light given up by narrowing the aperture or speeding up the shutter can be balanced by taking a stop back on one of the other two controls.[^stops-origin]

blocks.caption: Exposure controls for a single scene, with a meter showing how far the brightness sits from the target
blocks.task: Change one control to shift the exposure, then restore the brightness using a different control

parts.title: Superzoom reach and its optical cost

blocks.text: The P950's zoom lens spans an equivalent focal length range from 24 mm to 2000 mm, which makes it practical for distant wildlife.[^equivalent] Zooming in leaves your distance to the animal unchanged; instead, the lens narrows the angle of view so that a small fraction of the scene is stretched across the whole sensor. Stretching that narrow wedge of light magnifies the bird, and with it every wobble of your hands, any heat shimmer rising off warm ground, and the light loss from the lens's narrower maximum f-number at full extension.

blocks.caption: An animal across a field, viewed from 24 mm to 2000 mm equivalent
blocks.task: Zoom in until the animal fills half the height of the frame

blocks.caption: The widest available f-number across the zoom range
blocks.task: Zoom past 1200 mm and read the widest aperture the lens allows

blocks.text: Every superzoom lens carries a built-in optical trade-off at full extension: at 2000 mm the P950 can open no wider than f/6.5, which lets in nearly two and a half stops less light per unit area than f/2.8 at the wide end, just when the lens magnifies every tremor of your hands 83 times more than it does at 24 mm and so demands a much faster shutter speed. When you shoot at 2000 mm in Bird-watching mode, the camera makes up for that missing light by pushing the ISO up behind the scenes.

blocks.title: Stops and superzoom limits
points: One stop halves or doubles the light or amplification.
Full zoom costs light and magnifies shake.

blocks.caption: Questions on exposure, focus, and zoom
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.question: A photograph comes out smeared across the entire frame, including the tree branches and the background. Which problem caused the blur?
options: The camera moved while the shutter was open
The bird moved while the shutter was open
The ISO was set too high for the light
The aperture was set too wide
items.why: When stationary branches smear along with the bird, the camera itself moved during the exposure.

items.question: You narrow the aperture from f/2.8 to f/5.6. Which adjustment keeps the image at the same brightness?
options: Two stops more from a slower shutter or higher ISO
Nothing, because the exposure stays the same
A shutter speed two stops faster than before
A change of white balance to match the light
items.why: Narrowing from f/2.8 to f/4 halves the light (one stop), and f/4 to f/5.6 halves it again (a second stop), so the shutter must stay open four times as long or the ISO must quadruple.

items.question: How does raising the ISO setting brighten a dark image?
options: It amplifies the signal the sensor already caught, roughness and all
It makes the silicon sensor catch a bigger share of incoming photons
It opens the lens wider to let more light reach the sensor
It holds the shutter open for longer to collect more light
items.why: A sensor's photon sensitivity is fixed; raising ISO multiplies the weak signal read out from a small photon count, turning a dim, noisy measurement into a bright, grainy picture.

items.question: Why does a small-sensor camera like the P950 tend to keep backgrounds sharp unless you take specific steps to blur them?
options: Its small sensor uses short real focal lengths
Its lens glass is not sharp enough to separate planes
Its zoom range is too short for most wildlife
Its shutter speed cannot go slow enough
items.why: Because the sensor measures 6.17 by 4.55 mm, the lens uses short physical focal lengths whose openings in millimetres stay small unless you zoom in and pick a distant background.

items.question: At the 2000 mm equivalent zoom setting, the P950 lens opens no wider than f/6.5. What practical consequence follows from this limit?
options: Less light gets in, so the shutter slows or the ISO rises
The depth of field gets deeper, which cures motion blur
Nothing, since the lens gathers extra light when zoomed
The picture becomes completely free of photon noise
items.why: At f/6.5 the image on the sensor is dimmer, so the camera must slow the shutter or raise the ISO just when full zoom magnifies every wobble of your hands.

summary: **A soft background is mostly about distance.** The farther the background sits behind the subject, the more it blurs; the long end of the zoom helps most when the background is far away.
**Four controls shape every photograph.** Aperture, shutter speed, ISO and focus.
**Scene modes choose for you.** They set all four automatically, without showing what they gave up.
**A stop is a factor of two.** One stop halves or doubles the light, so stops can be traded between aperture, shutter speed and ISO.
**Shake blurs everything; motion blurs the subject.** Camera shake smears the whole frame, while a moving animal blurs alone.
**Grain comes from counting too few photons.** Random variation in a small count shows as noise.
**Zooming in costs light and steadiness.** The long end narrows the widest aperture and magnifies every wobble of your hands.

p950-specs.title: The Nikon Coolpix P950
p950-specs.text: Every interactive figure in this course uses the Nikon Coolpix P950's real specifications: a 1/2.3-inch sensor measuring 6.17 by 4.55 mm, and a 4.3 to 357 mm lens (24 to 2000 mm equivalent) with a maximum aperture that narrows from f/2.8 at the wide end to f/6.5 at the telephoto end. Another camera would shift the exact numbers while obeying the same physical rules.

aperture-etymology.title: Lens and aperture
aperture-etymology.text: The word *aperture* comes from the Latin *apertura*, meaning an opening. *Lens* comes from the Latin name for the lentil, because a double-convex piece of glass is shaped like a lentil bean.

circle.title: Circle of confusion
circle.text: Opticians call the blurred disc formed by an out-of-focus point the **circle of confusion**. The largest disc that still looks like a crisp point in a standard viewing print is conventionally taken as the sensor's diagonal divided by about 1500, which works out to roughly 0.005 mm on the P950's 7.66 mm diagonal compared with 0.029 mm on a 36 by 24 mm full-frame sensor.

muybridge.title: Freezing the gallop
muybridge.text: Early photographic plates needed seconds of light, turning every moving animal into a ghost. In 1878, Eadweard Muybridge used mechanical shutters triggered by tripwires at roughly 1/1000 of a second to photograph a galloping horse at Palo Alto, California, proving that a galloping horse lifts all four hooves off the ground at once, tucked beneath its belly rather than stretched out like a rocking horse.

shot-noise.title: Shot noise
shot-noise.text: Because photons arrive independently at random intervals, a count of N photons carries a natural statistical uncertainty equal to the square root of N. Collecting 10,000 photons yields a standard deviation of 100 (or 1%), whereas collecting 100 photons yields a variation of 10 (or 10%). Physicists call this **shot noise** (or Poisson noise, after Siméon Denis Poisson); Walter Schottky first analysed the same effect in the current through vacuum tubes in 1918, and the English name translates his German *Schroteffekt*, from *Schrot*, small lead shot.

iso-history.title: ASA, DIN, and ISO
iso-history.text: ISO stands for the International Organization for Standardization, which in 1974 merged the American ASA film speed scale and the German DIN scale into a single standard. A film photographer changed ISO by loading a different film; a digital camera has one sensor with a fixed ability to catch photons, so turning the ISO dial changes the electronic gain applied to its signal instead.

stops-origin.title: Waterhouse stops
stops-origin.text: Before lenses had built-in iris diaphragms, photographers adjusted the aperture by sliding brass plates with holes of different diameters into a slot in the lens barrel. Invented by John Waterhouse of Halifax, England, in 1858, these inserts were called *Waterhouse stops*, and photographers still say they "stop down" a lens when they close the aperture.

equivalent.title: Equivalent focal length
equivalent.text: A lens's physical focal length only tells you its angle of view once you know the size of the sensor behind it. Camera makers quote **35 mm equivalent focal length**, which is the focal length a 36 by 24 mm full-frame camera would need to frame the same view. Because the P950's sensor has a diagonal 5.65 times smaller than a full-frame sensor (a crop factor of 5.65), its 357 mm maximum focal length frames the same tight view as a 2000 mm lens on a full-frame camera.
